headline: Disapproved 47 Congress Street subdivision; approved 59 Boston Street site plan; recommended data center and two-family parking zoning changes to City Council.
summary: The board continued hearings for Harborlight Homes' Margin Street project, 57 Wharf Street, 75 North Street, and 11 Summer Street to October 15, 2026. It approved the 59 Boston Street decision and changes to the 40 Bridge Street decision, and it disapproved the 47 Congress Street preliminary subdivision plan. It recommended two zoning amendments to the City Council.
decisions: Extended the project deadline by forty-five days for the Harborlight Homes project on Margin, Endicott, and High Streets, 5-0 with one abstention.
Continued the Harborlight Homes public hearing to October 15, 2026, 5-0 with one abstention.
Continued the 57 Wharf Street Units UCB and UCC and 201 Derby Street hearing to October 15, 2026, 5-0 with one recusal.
Approved the decision for Pediatric Associates at 59 Boston Street (Map 15, Lot 321), 6-0.
Continued the 75 North Street (Map 26, Lot 58) hearing to October 15, 2026, 6-0.
Disapproved the Form B/Preliminary Subdivision application for 47 Congress Street (Map 34, Lot 448), 6-0.
Approved changes to the 40 Bridge Street site plan decision, pending other department issues within the 35-day window, 6-0.
Continued the 11 Summer Street hearing to October 15, 2026, 6-0.
Extended the Site Plan Review and Planned Unit Development Special Permit for 38 Norman Street to April 14, 2028, 6-0.
Recommended to City Council adoption of the data center zoning amendment with added text from the City Solicitor, and a working group, 6-0.
Recommended to City Council a zoning amendment amending Section 5 to require no parking for two-family dwelling units, 6-0.

A. 56 Margin Street, 54 Margin Street, 7 High Street, 20 Endicott Street (Map 25, Lot 
597), 24 Endicott Street (Map 25, Lot 595)  
Applicant: Harborlight Homes and Lifebridge North Shore  
Description: A continuation of a public hearing for all persons interested in the 
application of Harborlight Homes and Lifebridge North Shore at 56, 54 Margin 
Street, 20 Endicott Street, 7 High Street (Map 25, Lot 597) and 24 Endicott Street 
(Map 25, Lot 595) in the Residential Two-Family District (R2), Coastal Resilience 
Overlay District (C-ROD), Flood Hazard Overlay District (FHOD), and Smart Growth 
Overlay District (SGOD) for Smart Growth Overlay Plan Review and Coastal 
Resilience Overlay Site Plan Review in accordance with the following sections of the 
Salem Zoning Ordinance: Section 7.4 Smart Growth Overlay District and Section 8.9 
Coastal Resiliency Overlay District. Specifically, the applicant proposes the 
demolition of the buildings at 24 Endicott Street (Map 25, Lot 595) and 56 Margin 
Street (Map 25, Lot 597), the adaptive reuse of 54 Margin Street (Map 25, Lot 597), 
and the preservation of the façade of 20 Endicott Street (Map 25, Lot 597) to 
accommodate for a 22,806 square foot building comprised of 53 affordable homes, a 
shelter with 70 beds, and supportive programing space along with other site 
improvements. Thirteen parking spaces are proposed on site.  
 
CITY OF SALEM

Minutes September 17, 2026 
Page 2 of 16

through § 2-2033. 
 
Pat Connolly of Harborlight Homes and Stefano Basso of SV Design are in attendance 
for the applicant.  
 
The team has been working through the civil peer review, hoping to have something 
for  October 15, 2026.  
 
Mr. Basso shares his screen. On the memorial yard. They had a site visit with the 
Design Review Board (DRB) and community members and are making progress with 
the design. The egress has moved in to free up space for the memorial yard, losing a 
couple of parking spaces; the yard is smaller but in same location as current. The 
bell, benches, bricks, and WWII memorial will stay. They may add plaques to tell the 
history of the site. The yard now measures 28’ x 17’ x 9’. The egress from fire stairs 
comes through this way. The exterior siding has been lightened; the site visit led to a 
different color selection.  
 
Public Comment 
 
None 
 
Planning Board Comments 
 
Ms. Sides finds this much improved. She went on the DRB walk and feels the project 
is  going in the right direction. The memorial yard changes seem to be an 
improvement, even to what is there currently. Recommends removing the wood 
panes between windows. Mr. Basso asks if there is another detail to add or simpler 
façade? Ms. Sides says simpler façade, it fits in the neighborhood more now.  
 
Ms. Eimert mentions again that she is not voting but offers that the team has been 
working with the neighborhood as evidenced with the memorial yard.  
 
A motion to extend the project deadline for forty-five days is made by Tom Furey, seconded by 
Josh Turiel, and passes 5-0, with one abstention.

Same footprint for the most part. Tower is less tall than existing. Alley between

shingles and metal material.  
 
The team is working on the landscape plan. There is not much space to add street 
trees but will add where they can on Derby Street (honey locust). Proposed native

Ms. Sides on signage. The signage is too big. Would like to see some of the signage

Ms. Eimert appreciates the ramps, but it is not clear how they connect with parking

Mr. Grover says there is urgency to open this as they are being forced out of their

Ms. Cunningham shares her screen. The Board of Health has not provided review so

Ms. Obendorf shares her screen. A preliminary plan was filed under Section 3.a of the 
City of Salem Subdivision Regulations in order to preserve the owner's right under the 
zoning bylaw that are in place today. The plan is fully compliant with the subdivision 
regulations and the zoning bylaw. The applicant plans to file a definitive plan in a timely 
fashion. 
 
Planning Board Comments 
 
Ms. Sides asks if this proposal is going through a current building and should they be 
hearing about the demo of the building? Ms. Obendorf acknowledges that the building 
will need to be removed if this goes forward.  
 
Ms. Eimert pushes back that the Form B meets requirements. )ne of the charges put 
before us under the subdivision control on in the local regulations is to “ensure the 
provision of adequate access to all the lots in a subdivision by ways that will be safe and 
convenient for travel.” She understands that this is more related to an action that the 
subdivision filing created. But not practical in any way. Finds it  deficient in any realistic 
way to receive a Form C on this plan. Ms. Obendorf says it is just a preliminary plan, 
adequate access to proposed lots would be included in the definitive.  
 
Ms. Sides needs clarification. Mr. Berk says that they saw this with Bertini’s where it 
was done to freeze the zoning.  
 
Mr. Turiel is not sure where this is effective – an existing site without an approved 
plan to move forward? If there was a subdivision, he wants it in conjunction with a 
set plan. We don’t have a plan or filing.  
 
Ms. Cunningham shares her screen. The board should make a finding on if they  find 
that the filing provides adequate information per Mass General Law Ch.41, Sec 81.L 
and how the plan does or does not comply with Salem subdivision regulations. Ms. 
Cunningham shares Ch.41, Sec. 81.L.  
 
Mr. Turiel asks to see the plan again. Ms. Eimert asks about the grading of the 
proposed roadway. Ms. Obendorf says that it slopes to the cul-de-sac and away from 
public way with preliminary drainage system; grades are being maintained as are 
existing drainage patterns. Ms. Eimert says that the drainage area is sufficient to 
catch roadway runoff without affecting the adjacent body of water; Ms. Obendorf 
says yes. 
 
Ms. Sides says that she has seen the plans for Shetland Park and wonders why they 
cannot see the plan and understand better what is going on.

Ms. Eimert thinks that the preliminary plan is to be shared with other departments, 
including fire, and she is wondering about life safety access. Ms. Cuningham does 
not believe this has been received. Ms. Obendorf says the diameter of cul-de-sac is 
compliant.  
 
Ms. Cunningham shares the subdivision regulations. Ms. Eimert on section 2 – 
struggles with the idea the identifying the plans problems and planning for a future 
Form C.  
 
Ms. Sides thinks consideration should be given to the “attractiveness of the street 
layout in order to obtain the maximum livability and amenity of the subdivision.” 
Doesn’t see any context. 
 
Mr. Furey brings up rotaries and says that this is a major rotary and thinks this would 
be dangerous. Ms. Obendorf says that it is a dead end cul-de-sac, not a rotary. 
 
Mr. Turiel is not comfortable approving without what comes next. Ms. Cunningham 
says the board should look at does this provides adequate information as prescribed 
by the definition of a preliminary plan; and with what is provided, does the Board 
feel any of the language in the decision is untrue or should there be 
additions/modifications. Ms. Sides does not find that shows attractive street layout 
or maximum livability of the subdivision.  
 
Ms. Cunningham reiterates that the Board needs to determine if they think that this 
meets the definition of a preliminary plan, as state in Mass General Law.

G. 11 Summer Street (Map 26, Lot 459), 5-9 Summer Street (Map 26, Lot 461), and 15

Applicant: West House LLC, Emmerton House LLC, and Peabody House LLC,  
Description: A public hearing for all persons interested in the application of West House 
LLC, Emmerton House LLC, and Peabody House LLC, all d/b/a The Salem Inn, located at 
5,7,9 Summer Street (Map 26, Lot 459), 11-13 Summer Street (Map 26, Lot 461), and 15 
Summer Street (Map 26, Lot 462) in the B5 – Central Development district and Urban 
Renewal Overlay for Site Plan Review in accordance with Section 9.5 of the Salem 
Zoning Ordinance. Specifically, the applicant proposes the renovation of the existing 3 
story building at 11 Summer Street to accommodate a hotel with 16 units. The applicant 
is proposing site renovations including an increase of parking, through exterior parking 
changes, and renovations of the existing 2 story garage. Other site improvements 
include landscape improvements, and solar car ports. 
 
Attorney Scott Grover, Dan Ricciarelli and Julia Moradian of Seger, Michael Blier of 
Landworks Studio, and Katie Olyha of Stonefield Engineering are in attendance for the 
applicant. Dick Pabich, owner, is also in attendance.  
 
Have been to the Salem Redevelopment Authority (SRA) and the DRB.  
 
Ms. Olyha shares her screen. The improvements will be at 11 Summer Street. Access to 
the site is currently from Summer Street and nothing is changing. Predominantly 
imperious coverage under current conditions. Project proposes renovations of primary 
building and the accessory carriage house. Installation of solar carports, off street 
parking, EV charging stations, pocket park, drainage and utilities improvements as well. 
They are evaluating geothermal as well. Ingress one-way from Summer Street with one-
way circulation through site and egress at 15 Summer Street. There will be twenty three 
23 parking spaces proposed (one [1] in the garage of the carriage house. There will be a 
reduction of impervious coverage in the area. The modifications should provide an 
improvement overall.  
 
Mr. Blier says the circulation through the site creates a campus feel and a sense of 
cohesion of this area of Summer Street. There is a continuity of planting along Summer

Street and a reduction of pavement in front of the buildings to create a Salem Inn 
garden.  
 
Mr. Ricciarelli discusses existing building and says that they will restore the building back 
to its original Federal style. The inn will be fifteen (15) units and fully accessible. There 
will be a ramp on the exterior to get in the building. Have been to the Historical 
Commission for a Waiver of Demolition Delay (WDDO). They will be retaining the 
carriage house and will have schematic approval with DRB and SRA.  
 
Public Comment 
 
11 Summer Street Public Comment 09.17.26  
 
Planning Board Comments 
 
Mr. Furey praises the Pabich family and the proposed project.  
 
Ms. Sides compliments the team thinks it looks great and likes the one way parking.  
 
Mr. Turiel is enthusiastic about this project but points out that any work requiring 
access to an abutting property must be arranged with the abutter, they cannot walk on.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            
 
Ms. Eimert says that it is a beautiful project but asks how parking is currently provided. 
Mr. Pabich says that it is difficult. There are eleven (11) spaces and Curwen house on 
Essex Street has 17 spaces. Additionally, they rent spots at Riley Plaza and rely a little on 
on-street parking. This plan will make it easier. Ms. Eimert clarifies that the idea is that 
the center property will help manage parking needs of adjacent properties. She stresses 
that compact spaces can get tricky as cars are larger and these spaces do not always 
work out. Tandem spaces, one with an EV charging station, can also be tricky for guests.  
Mr. Ricciarelli says the spaces are parallel, not tandem. 
 
Mr. Wing appreciates the renovation and wonders if they are going fully electric? (Yes)/ 
Mr. Pabich says that the only gas they have right now is for hot water. Using a 
geothermal system for that function in the future. Hoping to provide enough solar to 
power that and hoping to be net zero. Mr. Wing asks if there is any need for any pruning

Ms. Eimert is curious if employees bike to work and if they will have bike parking. They 
do have bike parking. Mr. Pabich says that the staff is encouraged to no bring their cars

Mr. Turiel says that data centers themselves are not a major problem they 
exist in Salem already and are essential to business operations. And there are 
differences between types of data centers. The work has been surrounding, 
not banning a company with a server room, etc. The issue with a data center 
is with what are hyper-scaler data centers dedicated to artificial intelligence 
processing that consume ten (10) to twenty (20) times as much power as a 
regular server and cost exponentially more. They also require intensive 
cooling. Trying to craft the definition as to where the line is between a 
normal business use v. large AI data center. Salem does not have the 
resources or space to support a hyper-scaler data center. He has been 
working with the City Solicitor and the Planning Department to define the 
line. The basic divider he came up with is a combination of approximately 
one (1) or more than five thousand (5000) square feet of space being used or 
approximately two (2) megawatts of power. One (1) server of the type 
commonly used in hyper-scale centers is consuming three thousand (3000) – 
four thousand (4000) watts of power. You cannot fit that many in a two (2) 
megawatt hosting service. These limits will not attract large scale operations.  
 
Ms. Sides asks Mr. Turiel if by limiting physical space, we are taking into 
account smaller more efficient machines into small spaces. With language we 
need to be vague but strong. Wonders if applying specific numbers is the way 
to define it. Wonders about future technology that allows for more power 
draws in smaller spaces. Mr. Turiel says that the smaller the processor, the 
more concentrated the heat. There are three (3) sorts of things processed in 
data centers: storage uses, general computing, compute intensive 
application. The guide post is more or less  the Verizon building in 
downtown. Ms. Sides asks how the building handles cooling. Mr. Turiel says 
that they have generators that run periodically if there is an extended power 
outage. They also have batteries, so they don’t have to do that. They don’t 
need extensive cooling because they are not doing intensive tasks.  
 
Mr. Wing asks if thy put a limit on size/power, setting a cap makes an 
incentive to be more efficient.  
 
Ms. Eimert says a lot of communities are looking at this right now. And there 
is interest to moving toward defining by electrical demand. She would be 
interested in seeing revised language. Sounds like the conversation is 
creating a distinction between acceptable future sites v. unacceptable 
threshold curious how they revise the language to get from a proposal that 
has a definition to a use allowance that this is banned throughout the city.

Ms. Rennard says there is a phrase added after the first sentence of the 
definition and added a phrase “and has and aggregate power demand of two 
(2) megawatts or higher.” The recommendation needs to stay in the four 
corners of what was proposed. In looking at other communities, a lot have 
tiers addressing size and power usage.  She thinks this is where the city needs 
to head and Thinks this needs more thought and more IT professionals 
around the table to come up with a subsequent amendment. Mr. Turiel has 
been discussing the idea of a special permit for uses that draw one (1) to two 
(2) megawatts of power; this was not mentioned in the advertising of the 
public hearing and therefore outside of the four corners. Ms. Eimert says that 
the concern then is if we say they are not data centers then they don’t 
require a special permit, but if  we're saying that those facilities are not data 
centers, which is what we are doing through this amendment, then they 
don't require a special permit. She doesn’t see where they would be allowed 
in the city. Mr. Turiel says that way that this was initially written and 
advertised is constraining. Recommends looking at what Mansfield has done, 
that is the direction Salem should go in. But this step the way it has been 
written keeps away a large center being brought in.  
 
Mr. Berk says options are to recommend as is, recommend  with Mr. Turiel’s 
changes and a year on a committee, or rejection and having a more formal 
process as to what a data center is. Mr. Turiel says there is a need for a next 
step to go back in with proposal that looks like Mansfield. If we recommend 
what the solicitor put in, the immediate issue is removed and there is time 
for a long-term solution. 
 
Ms. Sides asks for clarification as to the addition of language regarding size. 
Mr. Turiel says that putting size in puts the risk of stepping on edge of four 
corners. If we start with what has been recommended and come back and 
work on square footage definitions, etc. Ms. Sides asks if Ms. Eimert is 
satisfied with this? Ms. Eimert thinks that is a wise path. Struggling with what 
this ends up looking like but thinks this needs far more scrutiny beyond how 
this was advertised. Ms. Rennard says that with this addition, would have 
data center generating over two (2) megawatts, then data center using less 
than, and where would those be allowed. Thinks these needs thought and 
don’t see the changes being in the four corners and need to readvertise. Ms. 
Eimert asks if as written, does the “primarily designed or used to house” 
language mean that like the hospital could expand. Mr. Turiel says that the 
language is related to information technology. Mr. Berk asks what if the 
hospital needs an off-site server facility? Mr. Turiel says it is more likely that 
it is regular business operation; the hospital has its own server site at Mass 
General in Boston and most of the hospital’s data is in the cloud.
